notes.meaning: Samuel speaks to all Israel as they gather to confirm Saul's kingship. He reminds them that he listened to everything they demanded and gave them an earthly ruler. He wants them to realize that having a king was their own choice, not God's original plan for them.

Samuel points out King Saul standing before them ready to lead. Samuel explains that he is now an old man with gray hair, and his sons are among the crowd as ordinary citizens rather than rulers. He has served the nation faithfully from his childhood until that very day.

Samuel puts his own life and leadership on trial before God and the king, who was God's anointed—someone specially chosen and marked by God with oil. He asks the crowd if he has ever stolen an animal, cheated or hurt anyone, or taken money to look the other way. If he has wronged anyone, he promises to pay it back immediately.

The people speak up and confirm that Samuel has never wronged or mistreated them. He had never taken bribes or used his position to steal from anyone. His public service had been completely honest and blameless.

Samuel calls on the Lord and the new king as official witnesses that his hands are clean of any wrongdoing. The crowd agrees that God is their witness. This proved that Israel had no good reason to complain about Samuel's leadership when they demanded a king.

Samuel reminds the assembly that the Lord is the one who appointed Moses and Aaron. It was God who rescued their ancestors from slavery in Egypt. True rescue has always come from the Lord, not from human rulers.

Samuel calls the people to stand still so he can reason with them before the Lord. He wants to review all the righteous acts God did for them and their ancestors. These acts were times God kept His promises and showed them undeserved mercy.

Samuel begins the history lesson with Jacob's family moving to Egypt and their descendants crying out when they were treated cruelly. God heard their cries and sent Moses and Aaron to bring them out of Egypt. The Lord then guided them safely into their own land.

After settling in the land, the people forgot the Lord and turned away from Him. Because of their sin, God allowed enemies like Sisera, the Philistines, and the king of Moab to defeat them. God used these hardships as discipline to turn their hearts back to Him.

When suffering under their enemies, the people realized their mistake and confessed their sins. They admitted that they had abandoned God to worship false Canaanite gods called the Baals and Ashtoreths. They begged God to deliver them and promised to serve Him alone.

The Lord answered their prayers by sending leaders like Gideon, Jephthah, and Samuel himself to deliver them. Each time, God freed them from their enemies so they could live in safety. This showed that God never failed to protect them when they trusted Him.

When King Nahash of the Ammonites attacked, the people panicked instead of trusting God. They demanded a human king to lead them into battle, forgetting that the Lord was already their true King. Their request showed that they had lost confidence in God's rule.

Samuel presents Saul as the leader the people requested and chose for themselves. At the same time, it was the Lord who set him in place over the nation. God granted their wish, but they were still under His divine authority.

Samuel tells the people that their future depends on honoring God. If both the people and their new king respect the Lord, obey His voice, and follow Him, things will go well. Having an earthly king did not replace their need to obey God.

Samuel warns that if they rebel and refuse to obey the Lord, God's hand will fight against them just as it fought against their ancestors. A human king could never protect them from the consequences of turning away from God. No nation can escape God's justice by changing its government.

Samuel tells the crowd to stand still and watch a great wonder God is about to perform. He wants them to pay close attention with their own eyes. The sign will prove that his words carry God's power and truth.

It was the time of the wheat harvest in early summer, a season when rain never fell in that region. Samuel announces that he will pray for thunder and rain right then. This miracle will show the people how terrible their sin was when they demanded an earthly king.

Samuel calls on the Lord, and God immediately sends crashing thunder and heavy rain out of a clear sky. The sudden storm terrifies the people. They are struck with deep awe and respect for both the Lord and His prophet.

Fearing for their lives, the people beg Samuel to pray to God on their behalf. They finally admit their deep guilt and confess that asking for a king was a great sin added to all their past wrongs. They see that they need God's mercy to survive.

Samuel tells the people not to be paralyzed by fear. Even though they had sinned greatly, they must not walk away from God now. Instead, they need to turn back and serve the Lord with all their hearts.

Samuel warns the nation not to wander after worthless idols. False gods are completely empty and have no power to help, protect, or rescue anyone in times of trouble. Putting trust in anything other than the true God always leads to disappointment.

Samuel comforts them with the promise that God will never abandon His people, for the honor of His own great name. God chose Israel out of His own free love and goodness, not because they had earned it. His faithfulness is rooted in His own character.

Samuel states that it would be a sin against the Lord if he stopped praying for the people. Even though they rejected him as their judge, he promises to keep interceding for them—praying to God on their behalf—and teaching them the good and right way to live.

Samuel urges the people to revere God and serve Him sincerely with their whole heart. They should look back and remember all the wonderful things the Lord had already done for them. True obedience comes from a thankful heart that remembers God's past goodness.

Samuel ends his address with a clear and serious warning. If the people stubbornly continue to do evil, both they and their new king will be swept away in judgment. An earthly king cannot save a people who refuse to obey God.
